subject: English
stem: He said to me, “You are getting lazy day by day.”
optA: He informed me that I am getting lazy day by day.
optB: He told me that I have been getting lazy day by day.
optC: He told me that I was getting lazy day by day.
optD: He told me that you were getting lazy day by day.
solution: A statement is reported with 'told'; the present continuous 'are getting' shifts to past continuous 'was getting', and 'you' becomes 'I'. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: “When will I be able to vote?” I asked my mother.
optA: I asked my mother when would he be able to vote.
optB: I asked to my mother when I will be able to vote.
optC: I asked my mother when I would be able to vote.
optD: I asked my mother when would I be able to vote.
solution: A reported question takes statement word order (subject before verb), 'will' becomes 'would', and 'I' stays 'I'. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: I said, “Father, when will you buy me a motor cycle?”
optA: I asked my father when will he buy me a motorcycle.
optB: I asked my father when he will buy me a motor cycle.
optC: I asked my father when would he buy me a motor cycle.
optD: I asked my father when he would buy me a motor cycle.
solution: The reported question keeps statement order ('when he would buy'), with 'will' shifting to 'would' and 'you' becoming 'he'. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: He said to me, “Is there any possibility of my getting promotion this year?”
optA: He asked me if there was any possibility of my getting promotion this year.
optB: He asked me if there was any possibility of his getting promotion this year.
optC: He asked me if there was any possibility of his getting promotion that year.
optD: He asked me if there is any possibility of his getting promotion this year
solution: In reported speech the yes/no question takes 'if', 'is' backshifts to 'was', 'my' becomes 'his', and 'this year' shifts to 'that year'. Option C applies all of these. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: The dealer said, “Either make your purchases or walk out of my shop.”
optA: The dealer told the customer that he would either make his purchases or walk out of his shop.
optB: The dealer ordered the customer to make his purchases and walk out of his shop.
optC: The dealer told the customer that he should either make his purchases, or walk out of his shop.
optD: The dealer requested the customer to make his purchases or walk out of his shop.
solution: The 'either...or' imperative is reported with 'should', and 'your/my' become 'his'. Option B wrongly changes 'or' to 'and', option D wrongly softens an order to a request, and option A drops the obligation sense. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: He said, “I do not wish to see any of you; go away.”
optA: He said that he had not wished to see any of them and ordered them to go away.
optB: He said that he did not wish to see any of them and ordered them to go away.
optC: He told that he did not wish to see any of them and ordered them to go away.
optD: He said that he does not wish to see any of us and ordered us to go away.
solution: 'Do not wish' shifts to 'did not wish', 'you' becomes 'them', and the imperative becomes 'ordered them to go away'. Option C misuses 'told' without an object and option D fails to shift the tense. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: He said to us, “Why are you all sitting about there doing nothing?”
optA: He asked us why are we all sitting about there doing nothing
optB: He asked us why we are all sitting about there doing nothing.
optC: He asked us why we were all sitting about there doing nothing.
optD: He asked us why were we all sitting about there doing nothing
solution: The reported wh-question keeps statement order ('why we were'), with 'are' shifting to 'were' and 'you' becoming 'we'. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: “May you live long and prosper”, said the old lady to her son.
optA: The old lady blessed her son with long life and wished him prosperity.
optB: The old lady prayed for her son’s long life and prosperity.
optC: The old lady prayed for her son and said that he might live long and prosper.
optD: The old lady blessed her son and prayed for his long life and prosperity.
solution: The optative 'May you live long and prosper' is reported with 'prayed that ... might ...' (may becomes might), preserving the wish. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: “Many happy returns of your birthday”, we said.
optA: We greeted him on his birthday.
optB: We said that many happy returns of your birthday.
optC: We wished him many happy returns of his birthday.
optD: We prayed for many happy returns of his birthday.
solution: An exclamatory good wish is reported with 'wished', and 'your' becomes 'his'. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: “Fie! a soldier and afraid of fighting!” said Babar.
optA: Babar exclaimed with surprise that a soldier should be afraid of fighting.
optB: Addressing a soldier, Babar cursed him that he should be afraid of fighting.
optC: Babar cursed the soldier who was afraid of fighting.
optD: Babar cursed and exclaimed that a soldier should not be afraid of fighting
solution: 'Fie!' expresses contempt and reproach (not mere surprise); the exclamation is reported as a curse that a soldier should not be afraid of fighting. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: OMIT
solution: 'Omit' means to leave out; its antonym is 'include' (to take in). 'Exclude' and 'add' are not direct opposites. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: INTEGRATION
solution: 'Integration' means combining into a whole; its antonym is 'fragmentation' (breaking into parts). The others are synonyms. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: MINIATURE
solution: 'Miniature' means very small; its antonym is 'large'. 'Small' is a synonym. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: EXHAUSTS
solution: 'Exhausts' means tires out or drains; its antonym is 'invigorates' (to give energy). 'Tires', 'empties' and 'drains' are synonyms. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: DISTANT
solution: 'Distant' means far away; its antonym is 'close'. 'Far' is a synonym. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: TRANSPARENT
solution: 'Transparent' means see-through/clear; its antonym is 'opaque' (not transparent). 'Clear' and 'crystal' are synonyms. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: ENCOUNTERED
solution: 'Encountered' means met or faced; its antonym is 'avoided'. 'Faced' is a synonym. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: HANDY
solution: Per the official key the answer is 'heavy'. (Note: the standard antonym of 'handy' is 'unwieldy' or 'cumbersome'; this key is questionable and is flagged for review.) Matches option D.
reviewNote: Aligned to official LWS key, but the key looks wrong (see solution); recommend the teacher verify the master.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: ELEGANCE
solution: 'Elegance' means grace and refinement; its antonym is 'vulgarity' (lack of taste and refinement). Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Choose the word OPPOSITE in meaning to: CAPRICIOUS
solution: 'Capricious' means changeable and unpredictable; its antonym is 'firm' (steady, constant). 'Fickle' is a synonym. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: When he saw the snake he took to his heels.
solution: 'Took to his heels' means ran away quickly, usually in fear. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: He has to abide by the hard and fast rule of the company.
solution: A 'hard and fast rule' is a strict, fixed rule that cannot be changed. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: She goes to her mother’s house off and on.
solution: 'Off and on' means from time to time, intermittently, i.e. occasionally. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: The robber murdered the woman in cold blood for the sake of the jewels.
optC: a murder done in great anger
solution: 'In cold blood' means done deliberately and without emotion or pity. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: Indians are going places in the field of software technology.
solution: 'Going places' means becoming successful or achieving distinction. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: The poet drew on his fancy, not his knowledge of Nature, when he wrote his poem on birds.
solution: 'Drew on his fancy' means relied on his imagination. The contrast with 'knowledge' confirms this. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: My neighbour had to pay through his nose for a brand new car.
solution: 'Pay through the nose' means to pay an unreasonably or excessively high price. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: Very ambitious people do not like to rest on their laurels.
solution: 'Rest on one's laurels' means to be satisfied with past success and stop striving, i.e. to be complacent. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: If he phones again, I am going to give him a piece of my mind.
solution: 'Give someone a piece of one's mind' means to rebuke or reprimand them angrily. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: The party high command wanted to stave off an open battle.
optC: allow it to take its own course
solution: 'Stave off' means to ward off or delay something undesirable; here, to postpone an open battle. Matches option A.
reviewNote: 'Postpone' (A) is a possible near-meaning, but 'stave off' primarily means to ward off/prevent, so D is the best fit.

subject: English
context: The Printing Press has made knowledge available to the vast multitude of people-Pray, what kind of knowledge is it? Is it of any permanent character? Books have become common and, when we say that books like the Sexton Blake series sell like hot cakes, we have an index of the nature of knowledge which a typical person in a vast multitude seeks. Let me tell you of an incident that took place in America a few years ago. An American publisher printed a million copies of the works of Charles Dickens in the hope that he could easily sell them on the name of the author. But to his disappointment, not even the widest publicity and advertisement could enable him to sell the books. Being sorely tired, he hit on a plan. He tore off the cover pages, substituted covers containing sensational love headings for the titles and again advertised the new books. In a week, all the books were sold out. We are not concerned here with the moral of the bookseller’s action. What we have to note is that only books of a sensational type are really sought for by the ordinary folk who have a great aversion to serious study. So, you will see that the grand argument that the Printing Press has made knowledge available even to the masses is certainly fallacious and quite misleading. To put it correctly, it has created a taste for a low order of books.
stem: Sexton Blake series are big sellers because they
solution: The passage states that only books of a sensational type are really sought for by ordinary readers, who shun serious study. Matches option D.

stem: The American publisher had chosen the works of Charles Dickens to
optA: give wide publicity to Dickens’ works.
optB: offer the readers what best he could.
solution: The passage says he printed a million copies 'in the hope that he could easily sell them on the name of the author' – i.e. to make money easily. Matches option D.

stem: What is the main contention of the passage?
optA: To stress the popularity of the printing press.
optB: To point out the disappointment of serious readers.
optC: To shed light on the morale of the publishers.
optD: To bring out the evil impacts of the printing press.
solution: The author argues the claim that the press spread knowledge is fallacious and that it has created a taste for low-order books – highlighting its harmful effect. Matches option D.

stem: Who is Charles Dickens?
solution: Charles Dickens was a celebrated English novelist. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Succession of rulers belonging to one family.
solution: A 'dynasty' is a line of hereditary rulers from one family. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: To cut something into two pieces.
solution: 'Sever' means to cut or divide into parts. 'Severe' is an adjective and the others are unrelated. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: Flat metal or Porcelain plate fixed on a wall as an ornament or memorial.
solution: A 'plaque' is an ornamental or commemorative flat plate fixed to a wall. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Act of deceiving somebody in order to make money.
solution: 'Fraud' is deception carried out for financial gain. Robbery and theft involve taking without deception. Matches option A.

subject: English
stem: A short poem or speech addressed to the spectators after the conclusion of a drama.
solution: An 'epilogue' is a concluding speech or poem at the end of a play. A 'prologue' comes at the beginning. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: The smugglers did not realise that their conversation was being recorded.
optA: The smugglers did not realise that someone was recording their conversation.
optB: Someone did not realise that the smugglers were recording their conversation.
optC: Conversation was recorded when the smugglers did not realise.
optD: The smugglers recorded their conversation without realising.
solution: The embedded passive clause 'their conversation was being recorded' converts to the active 'someone was recording their conversation', keeping the meaning intact. Matches option A.
reviewNote: The given sentence's clause is already passive; the correct transformation here is the active equivalent (option A), which is the only option preserving the original meaning.

subject: English
stem: The principal kept the staff members waiting.
optA: The staff members are kept waiting for the principal.
optB: The staff members were kept waiting by the principal.
optC: The staff members were waiting for the principal.
optD: The staff members were being kept waiting by the principal.
solution: The simple past active 'kept...waiting' becomes the simple past passive 'were kept waiting by the principal'. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: Who taught you grammar?
optA: By whom you were taught grammar?
optB: By whom were you taught grammar?
optC: By whom was grammar you taught?
optD: By whom were grammar taught to you?
solution: An active wh-question with 'who' as the agent becomes 'By whom were you taught grammar?' with correct interrogative word order. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: The king gave him a reward.
optA: He was given by the king a reward.
optB: He was given the reward by a king.
optC: He was given a reward by the king.
optD: A reward was given by him to the king.
solution: Taking the indirect object as subject, the passive is 'He was given a reward by the king', preserving the articles. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: He teaches us grammar.
optA: Grammar was taught to us by him.
optB: We are taught grammar by him.
optC: We were teached grammar by him.
optD: Grammar will be teached to us by him
solution: The simple present active 'teaches' becomes the simple present passive 'are taught'. Options C and D use the wrong form 'teached' and wrong tense. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: Rearrange the parts to form a coherent sentence. 1: A dictionary | P: arranged words | Q: about which information | R: containing alphabetically | S: is a book | 6: is given.
solution: The coherent sentence is: 'A dictionary is a book (S) containing alphabetically (R) arranged words (P) about which information (Q) is given.' Order S-R-P-Q. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: Rearrange the parts to form a coherent sentence. 1: Agriculture | P: cotton for our clothes | Q: raw materials like jute | R: and sugarcane for our industries | S: gives us food | 6: and food for cattle.
solution: The coherent sentence is: 'Agriculture gives us food (S), cotton for our clothes (P), raw materials like jute (Q) and sugarcane for our industries (R) and food for cattle.' Order S-P-Q-R. Matches option D.

subject: English
stem: Rearrange the parts to form a coherent sentence. 1: Today political freedom | P: and the right | Q: however money and all that money | R: assures people equality before law | S: to elect their Government | 6: can buy is not fairly distributed.
solution: The coherent sentence is: 'Today political freedom assures people equality before law (R) and the right (P) to elect their Government (S), however money and all that money (Q) can buy is not fairly distributed.' Order R-P-S-Q. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: Rearrange the parts to form a coherent sentence. 1: By far the most logical step | P: to relieve the housewife of routine | Q: which can be programmed | R: to carry out standard operations | S: is to provide a robot | 6: when switched by the housewife.
solution: The coherent sentence is: 'By far the most logical step to relieve the housewife of routine (P) is to provide a robot (S) which can be programmed (Q) to carry out standard operations (R) when switched by the housewife.' Order P-S-Q-R. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: Rearrange the parts to form a coherent sentence. 1: During the reign of the Emperor Tiberius | P: called Phaedrus | Q: an Augustan story teller | R: translated Aesop’s fables into Latin | S: in ancient Rome | 6: and also added some tales of his own.
solution: The coherent sentence is: 'During the reign of the Emperor Tiberius in ancient Rome (S) an Augustan story teller (Q) called Phaedrus (P) translated Aesop’s fables into Latin (R) and also added some tales of his own.' Order S-Q-P-R. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: Suppose a rod is given a negative charge by rubbing it with wool. Which one of the following statements is correct in this case ?
optA: The positive charges are transferred from rod to wool
optB: The positive charges are transferred from wool to rod
optC: The negative charges are transferred from rod to wool
optD: The negative charges are transferred from wool to rod
solution: When a rod is rubbed with wool, electrons (negative charges) transfer from the wool to the rod, giving the rod a negative charge; the wool becomes positively charged. Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one of the following can charge an insulator?
solution: Insulators can be charged by friction (static electricity), e.g. rubbing a glass rod. Current electricity flows through conductors, not insulators. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem:
Which of the following statements correctly explains/explain the existence of a positive force between two electric charges?
1. Both the charges are positive.
2. Both the charges are negative.
3. Both the charges are oppositely charged.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
solution: A repulsive (positive) force exists between like charges, both positive (statement 1) or both negative (statement 2). Oppositely charged bodies attract, so statement 3 is wrong. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one of the following is the best shape of a solid metal rod to form the top end of a lightning conductor ?
solution: Charge density is highest at sharp points, so a pointed/conical tip produces the greatest electric field, enabling corona discharge and attracting lightning. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: Lightning is due to
optA: The flow of charges between different parts of the cloud
optB: The short-circuiting of charges between the upper and lower surfaces of the cloud
optC: The collection of positively charged particles on the base and collection of negatively charged particles at the top of the cloud
optD: The induction of positive charge on the ground below the negative charge at the base of the cloud
solution: Per the official key, lightning is attributed to the induction of positive charge on the ground below the negative charge at the base of the cloud. (Note: the standard/bank answer is A, the flow of charges between different parts of the cloud; this key is flagged for review.) Matches option D.
reviewNote: Aligned to official LWS key, but the key looks wrong (see solution); recommend the teacher verify the master.

subject: Physics
stem: For a material under static conditions, which one among the following statements is correct ?
optB: A perfect conductor can be charged
optC: Both perfect conductor and insulator can be charged
optD: Both perfect conductor and insulator cannot be charged
solution: Under static conditions both a perfect conductor and an insulator can hold charge, so both can be charged. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: The work done in moving a charge of 2 coulomb (C) from point A to point B is 24 J. What is the potential difference between A and B?
solution: Potential difference V = W/Q = 24/2 = 12 V. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one of the following is NOT a basic property of electric charge?
optC: Charge on a body is always an integral multiple of an electron or a proton charge
optD: Charges can be created and destroyed in an isolated system
solution: Electric charge is conserved, it cannot be created or destroyed in an isolated system. Option D contradicts the law of conservation of charge. Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: Three equal resistors are connected in parallel configuration in a closed electrical circuit. Then the total resistance in the circuit becomes
optD: three times of the individual resistance.
solution: For n equal resistors R in parallel, 1/R_total = n/R, so R_total = R/n = R/3, i.e. one-third of each individual resistance. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: Two resistances of 5.0 ohm and 7.0 ohm are connected in series and the combination is connected in parallel with a resistance of 36.0 ohm. The equivalent resistance of the combination of three resistors is
solution: Series: 5 + 7 = 12 ohm. Parallel with 36 ohm: R_eq = (12*36)/(12+36) = 432/48 = 9 ohm. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: If three resistors of 1 Ohm each connect in parallel to each other the resultant resistance is
solution: For n equal resistors R in parallel, R_eq = R/n = 1/3 Ohm. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: The cost of energy to operate an industrial refrigerator that consumes 5 kW power working 10 hours per day for 30 days will be (Given that the charge per kW.h of energy = Rs 4)
solution: Energy = Power * Time = 5 kW * 10 hr/day * 30 days = 1500 kW.h. Cost = 1500 * Rs 4 = Rs 6,000. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem:
Water is heated with a coil of resistance R connected to domestic supply. The rise of temperature of water will depend on
1. Supply voltage.
2. Current passing through the coil.
3. Time for which voltage is supplied.
Select the correct answer from among the following:
solution: Heat produced H = VIt = I^2*R*t = V^2*t/R, so it depends on supply voltage, current and time. All three factors affect the temperature rise. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one of the following formulas does not represent electrical power ?
solution: Electrical power formulas are P = VI, P = I^2*R and P = V^2/R. The expression IR^2 has no standard power derivation and does not represent power. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: What is the current required to light a 60 W incandescent bulb in a domestic supply of 240 V?
solution: Using P = VI, I = P/V = 60/240 = 0.25 A. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: An electric bulb is connected to 220 V generator. The current drawn is 600 mA. What is the power of the bulb?
solution: 600 mA = 0.6 A. Power P = V*I = 220*0.6 = 132 W. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one of the following terms cannot represent electrical power in a circuit?
solution: Electrical power: P = VI = I^2*R = V^2/R. The term I^2/R does not have the units of power (Watts), so it cannot represent electrical power. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: In which one among the following situations, the bulb would glow the most ? (Consider all batteries are the same)
optB: 2 batteries in series, 2 bulbs in series
optD: 2 batteries in series, 2 bulbs in parallel
solution: With 2 batteries in series, 2 bulbs in parallel, each bulb gets the full doubled voltage, maximising power per bulb (P = V^2/R). Matches option D.
reviewNote: Paper prints the four options twice (a duplicate block); transcribed once.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: Which one of the following statements regarding magnetic field is NOT correct?
optA: Magnetic field is a quantity that has direction and magnitude
optB: Magnetic field lines are closed curves
optC: Magnetic field lines are open curves
optD: No two magnetic field lines are found to cross each other
solution: Magnetic field lines are always closed curves (closed loops, N to S outside and S to N inside a magnet); they are never open. Statement (c) is NOT correct. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: At which place Earth's magnetic field becomes horizontal ?
solution: At the magnetic equator the angle of dip (inclination) is zero, so Earth's magnetic field is entirely horizontal. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: The magnetic field strength of a current-carrying wire at a particular distance from the axis of the wire
optA: depends upon the current in the wire
optB: depends upon the radius of the wire
optC: depends upon the temperature of the surroundings
solution: By Ampere's law, the field B = mu0*I/(2*pi*r) depends on the current I and the distance r, not on the wire radius or ambient temperature. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: Imagine a current-carrying straight conductor with magnetic field of lines in anti-clockwise direction. Then the direction of current is determined by
optA: the Right-Hand Thumb rule and it would be in the downward direction.
optB: the Left-Hand Thumb rule and it would be in the downward direction.
optC: the Right-Hand Thumb rule and it would be in the upward direction.
optD: the Left-Hand Thumb rule and it would be in the upward direction.
solution: By the Right-Hand Thumb rule, if the fingers curl in the direction of the field (anti-clockwise viewed from above), the thumb points upward, so the current flows upward. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying straight wire at a point outside the wire depends
optA: inversely on the distance from it
optB: directly on the distance from it
optC: inversely at short distances and directly at large distances from it
optD: directly on the distance (at short distances) and inversely on the distance (at long distances) from it
solution: By the Biot-Savart law, the field of a long straight wire is B = mu0*I/(2*pi*r), which varies inversely with distance. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: What is the net force experienced by a bar magnet placed in a uniform magnetic field?
optB: Depends upon length of the magnet
solution: In a uniform magnetic field the forces on the N and S poles are equal and opposite, giving zero net force (though there may be a net torque). Matches option A.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: Which one of the following statements about magnetic field lines is NOT correct?
optA: They can emanate from a point
optB: They do not cross each other
optC: Field lines between two poles cannot be precisely straight lines at the ends
optD: There are no field lines within a bar magnet
solution: Magnetic field lines exist inside a bar magnet (running from S to N internally), so 'there are no field lines within a bar magnet' is NOT correct. Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following statements is not correct?
optA: Most carbon compounds are good conductors of electricity.
optB: Bonding in organic compounds is covalent.
optC: Graphite is used as a lubricant.
optD: Diamond is an allotrope of carbon.
solution: Most carbon (organic) compounds are poor conductors of electricity because their bonding is covalent with no free ions or mobile electrons (graphite is the notable exception). Bonding in organic compounds being covalent (B), graphite as a lubricant (C) and diamond as an allotrope of carbon (D) are all correct. The false statement is (a). Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: The number of structural isomers of pentane is
solution: Pentane \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\) has 3 structural isomers: n-pentane, isopentane (2-methylbutane) and neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane). Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
stem:
Which among the following statements with respect to carbon is/are correct?
1. Carbon forms the basis for all living organisms and many things we use
2. Carbon shows tetra-valency and the property of catenation
3. Carbon forms covalent bonds with itself and other elements
4. Carbon forms compounds containing triple and tetra bonds between carbon atoms

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: carbon is the basis of life, shows tetra-valency and catenation, and forms covalent bonds. Statement 4 is incorrect — carbon forms single, double and triple bonds but not quadruple ('tetra') bonds between carbon atoms. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Functional Groups and Common Organic Compounds
stem:
Consider the following statements:
I. Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.
II. Catenation and isomerism in carbon explain the large number of organic compounds.
III. Carbon dioxide is acidic but carbon monoxide is a neutral molecule.

Which are correct?
solution: I is correct (soaps are sodium/potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids). II is correct (catenation and isomerism account for the huge number of organic compounds). III is correct (\(\text{CO}_2\) is an acidic oxide while \(\text{CO}\) is a neutral oxide). All three are correct. Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct?
optA: Buckminsterfullerene is an allotrope of carbon
optB: Diamond is a good conductor of electricity
optC: Graphite is a good conductor of electricity
optD: In graphite, each carbon atom is linked to three other carbon atoms
solution: Diamond is an electrical insulator — all four valence electrons of each carbon are locked in covalent bonds, leaving none free to conduct. Buckminsterfullerene is an allotrope (A), graphite conducts (C) and each graphite carbon links to three others (D), all correct. The false statement is (b). Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
stem:
Molecules of which of the following has cage like structure ?
1. Diamond
2. Graphite
3. Fullerenes

Select the correct answer using the code given below :
solution: Fullerenes (e.g. \(\text{C}_{60}\)) have a closed cage-like (soccer-ball) structure. Diamond is a 3-D tetrahedral network and graphite is a layered planar sheet structure; neither is cage-like. Only fullerenes qualify. Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following elements is used in pencil-lead ?
solution: Pencil 'lead' contains no lead metal; it is made of graphite (an allotrope of carbon) mixed with clay. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following properties is NOT true for graphite?
optA: Hybridisation of each carbon atom is \(sp^3\)
optB: Hybridisation of each carbon atom is \(sp^2\)
optC: Electrons are delocalized over the whole sheet of atoms
optD: Each layer is composed of hexagonal rings
solution: In graphite each carbon is \(sp^2\) hybridised (three sigma bonds in a plane plus a delocalised p-electron). The claim that it is \(sp^3\) (option a) is therefore NOT true. Delocalised electrons (C) and hexagonal-ring layers (D) are correct. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following is the purest form of Carbon?
solution: Fullerene (e.g. Buckminsterfullerene \(\text{C}_{60}\)) is a well-defined molecular allotrope and is regarded as the purest form of carbon; charcoal, coke and carbon black are impure amorphous forms. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following statements is not correct?
optA: All carbons in diamond are linked by carbon-carbon single bond.
optB: Graphite is layered structure in which layers are held together by weak van der Waals forces.
optC: Graphite layers are formed by hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.
optD: Graphite layers are held together by carbon-carbon single bond.
solution: Within a graphite layer carbons are covalently bonded in hexagonal rings, but the layers themselves are held together only by weak van der Waals forces, NOT by carbon-carbon single bonds. Statement (d) is false. Diamond's single-bond network (A), van der Waals interlayer forces (B) and hexagonal-ring layers (C) are correct. Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following statements about diamond and graphite is not correct?
optA: Diamond has a tetrahedral structure, whereas graphite has a hexagonal planar structure.
optB: Both physical and chemical properties of diamond and graphite are different.
optC: Graphite is soft but diamond is hard.
optD: Graphite is a good conductor of electricity while diamond is not.
solution: Diamond and graphite are both allotropes of carbon, so they have identical chemical composition and therefore the same chemical properties; only their physical properties differ. The statement that BOTH physical and chemical properties differ (option b) is not correct. Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following materials is not an allotrope of carbon ?
solution: Diamond, graphene and fullerene are all allotropes of carbon. Fly ash is a fine residue from coal combustion (a mixture of oxides), not an allotrope of carbon. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following allotropes of carbon is isomorphous with crystalline silicon?
solution: Diamond has a tetrahedral covalent network identical in form to crystalline silicon, so the two are isomorphous. Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which among the following statements is not correct with respect to allotropes of Carbon?
optA: Graphite is a good conductor of electricity.
optB: Diamond is the hardest substance known.
optC: Fullerene is one of the allotropes of carbon.
optD: Next to diamond, graphite is the second hardest known substance.
solution: Graphite is soft and slippery, not hard — it is certainly not the second hardest substance. Graphite conducting (A), diamond being hardest (B) and fullerene being an allotrope (C) are correct. The false statement is (d). Matches option D.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Buckminster fullerene, which looks like a football, is an allotropic form of
solution: Buckminsterfullerene \(\text{C}_{60}\) is a spherical (football-shaped) molecule made entirely of 60 carbon atoms, so it is an allotrope of carbon. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
stem:
Match List-I (Allotrope of Carbon) with List-II (Property) and select the correct answer :
List-I: A. Graphite  B. Diamond  C. Fullerene  D. Graphene
List-II: 1. Thinnest and strongest material  2. Hardest natural substance  3. Very light and strong material  4. Soft and slippery material
solution: Graphite (A) is soft and slippery (4); Diamond (B) is the hardest natural substance (2); Fullerene (C) is very light and strong (3); Graphene (D) is the thinnest and strongest material (1). The pairing A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: The elemental composition of diamond is
solution: Diamond is an allotrope of carbon, composed entirely of carbon atoms in a tetrahedral covalent network — it is pure carbon. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following forms of carbon is thermodynamically most stable?
solution: Graphite has the lowest Gibbs free energy among carbon allotropes at standard conditions and is taken as the thermodynamically most stable (reference) form of carbon; diamond is metastable. Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct ?
optA: Diamond is hard due to extended covalent bonding in it
optB: Fullerene is composed of five and six membered rings
optC: Diamond is a good conductor of electricity
optD: Graphite is used as a lubricant
solution: Diamond is a poor conductor (an insulator) because all valence electrons are tied up in covalent bonds; it is hard for the same extended-bonding reason (A). Fullerene has five- and six-membered rings (B) and graphite is a lubricant (D), both correct. The false statement is (c). Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
stem: \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\) belongs to the homologous series of
solution: Alkenes have the general formula \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\); for \(n=4\) this gives \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\) (butene). The standard textbook classification of an open-chain \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\) places it in the alkene series. Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following is the chemical formula of gypsum?
solution: Gypsum is hydrated calcium sulphate, \(\text{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\). Plaster of Paris is \(2\text{CaSO}_4\cdot \text{H}_2\text{O}\) (the hemihydrate) and \(\text{CaSO}_4\) is the anhydrous form. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Functional Groups and Common Organic Compounds
stem: Which one of the following is an organic acid?
solution: Acetic acid \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\) is a carboxylic acid — a carbon-containing organic acid. HCl, \(\text{HNO}_3\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) are inorganic (mineral) acids. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Functional Groups and Common Organic Compounds
stem: What is the action of litmus on ethanol?
optB: Ethanol turns blue litmus to red; confirming acidic nature of ethanol
optC: Ethanol turns red litmus to blue; confirming basic nature of ethanol
optD: Ethanol decolorizes litmus through bleaching action
solution: Ethanol is a neutral compound; it neither turns blue litmus red nor red litmus blue, so litmus is neutral towards it. Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Litmus, a well-known acid-base indicator, is derived from :
solution: Litmus is a natural dye extracted from lichens (notably Roccella tinctoria). Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Functional Groups and Common Organic Compounds
stem: Which one among the following compounds has a sweet and fruity smell ?
solution: Esters have characteristic sweet, fruity smells. Ethyl acetate \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5\) is an ester used as a flavouring and in nail-polish remover. Matches option C.
